explanation: The correct answer is D (eyewire screw tightness and lens seating, confirming no rattle and no gap): the closing checks of standard bench alignment confirm that each screw is present, correctly threaded, and snug without being over torqued, and that each lens bevel is fully seated in the groove all the way round with no gap at the eyewire joint and no rattle. Vertex distance and temple bend position belong to the patient fitting task, not to the bench reference state. Face form, tilt, temple fold, and spread all sit earlier in the working order and are re checked rather than used to close the task.

question: A candidate goes straight to the face of the examiner acting as a patient with a metal frame that was handed over with one temple riding high on the bench. The front is bent until the frame looks level on the face. Why is this approach penalized even though the result looks level?

options.A: A frame fault has been hidden inside a fitting bend, so neither can be judged
options.B: The frame will no longer fold flat enough to fit inside a spectacle case
options.C: Bending a metal front on the face always cracks the plating at the bridge
options.D: Levelling the front is not a task the examiner scores in this part

explanation: The correct answer is A (a frame fault has been hidden inside a fitting bend, so neither can be judged): standard bench alignment is the reference condition, and until the frame is back in it there is no way to tell whether an observed fault belongs to the face or to the frame. Compensating for a high temple by twisting the front stacks one distortion on another, and the frame will look wrong again the moment anything else is touched. Folding into a case has nothing to do with the marking. Plating damage comes from serrated jaws and overworking rather than from levelling, and levelling the front is very much part of the scored task.

question: The candidate observes that the pupils sit above the vertical midline of each lens and the lower rim rests on the cheeks when the examiner smiles. The front is level and lash clearance is adequate. Which single change raises the frame without disturbing the pantoscopic tilt already set?

options.A: Bring the two nose pads closer together so they bear higher
options.B: Open the temple spread angle equally at both endpieces
options.C: Move both temple bends further back from the front
options.D: Increase the frontal angle of each pad by the same amount

explanation: The correct answer is A (bring the two nose pads closer together so they bear higher): pads set closer together ride higher up the wedge of the nose and lift the whole front, and because the change is made at the pads the tilt already set at the endpieces is untouched. Opening the temple spread angle loosens the grip at the sides and pushes the front forward rather than up. Moving the temple bends further back lets the frame slide down, which is the opposite of what is wanted. Altering the frontal angle changes how the pad face meets the skin from top edge to bottom edge, not the height at which the frame rides.

question: During a practice run the candidate sets the pads perfectly, then discovers the front needed levelling and changes it at the endpieces. The pads no longer bear evenly on an examiner who gives no feedback. What general principle does this illustrate for the thirty minute station?

options.A: Pads are set last because everything above them moves where they bear
options.B: Pads should be set twice, once before and once after the front
options.C: Pad angles must never be altered once the frame leaves the bench
options.D: Levelling the front should always be done with the pad arms alone

explanation: The correct answer is A (pads are set last because everything above them moves where they bear): the front and the temples decide where the frame sits, and every change to either of them lands the pads on a different part of the nose. Leaving the pads until the end means the bearing is set once, against a position that will not move again. Deliberately setting the pads twice wastes minutes in a station that gives only thirty for three tasks. Pad angles are adjusted on the face as a matter of course. Levelling with the pad arms alone hides a front fault instead of correcting it.

question: On a metal frame the candidate finds the lenses sitting too far from the eyes, with a wide gap between the back of the lens and the lashes. The frame is level and the pads bear evenly. Which two adjustments are available to shorten the vertex distance?

options.A: The temple spread angle at the endpieces and the pad arm position
options.B: The temple bend position and the frontal angle of each pad
options.C: The face form at the bridge and the temple fold angle
options.D: The eyewire screw tension and the vertical angle of each pad

explanation: The correct answer is A (the temple spread angle at the endpieces and the pad arm position): closing the angle where the temple leaves the front draws the front toward the face, and setting the pad arms so the pads sit further forward on the nose lets the front come in as well, so those two controls govern vertex distance on a metal frame. The temple bend position decides how far back the frame is held and how high it rides. Face form is horizontal wrap and temple fold is a bench check made off the face. Screw tension holds the lens, and the vertical angle only rotates the pad on the skin.

question: A metal frame slides down the nose on downgaze on the examiner acting as a patient. Its pads are set wide apart and bear only on their lower edges, and both temple ends are almost straight. Which action by the candidate would make the sliding worse instead of better?

options.A: Open the pads further apart so each one covers more skin
options.B: Bring the pads closer together and reset the frontal angles
options.C: Shape both temple ends to follow the head behind the ears
options.D: Recheck that each bend starts at the top of the ear

explanation: The correct answer is A (open the pads further apart so each one covers more skin): pads already set too wide are the reason the frame is running down the wedge of the nose, and separating them further lets it drop faster no matter how much skin each pad covers. Bringing the pads closer together and correcting the frontal angle puts the full pad face back on the nose and restores grip. Shaping the temple ends to follow the head gives the support that almost straight ends cannot. Confirming the bend position is a reasonable check as well, because a bend set too far back also allows a frame to slide.

question: After two minutes of wear the candidate removes the frame and looks at the skin. Behind the left ear the skin is white and takes several seconds to return to normal colour. Behind the right ear there is a faint pink line that fades at once. How should these be read?

options.A: Both sides show normal contact and neither needs any further work
options.B: Both sides are too tight and both temple ends must be relaxed
options.C: The right side is too tight and the left shows acceptable contact
options.D: The left side is too tight and the right shows acceptable contact

explanation: The correct answer is D (the left side is too tight and the right shows acceptable contact): blanching is blood driven out of the tissue, and slow return of colour confirms real pressure, so the left temple end is gripping harder than the skin can tolerate and must be relaxed. A faint pink line that fades immediately is the normal trace of light even contact and needs nothing done to it. Treating both sides as normal leaves a genuine pressure point on a patient who cannot report it. Relaxing both ends would loosen a side that is already correct and invite the frame to slide.

question: With the frame on the face the candidate sees the left lens sitting closer to the cheek than the right, although both temples are equal at the ears and the pads bear evenly. The frame was not checked on the bench beforehand. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: A twist in the front, leaving the two lens planes out of line
options.B: A difference in eyewire screw tension between the two sides
options.C: Unequal splay angles set on the two nose pads at the bridge
options.D: A left temple that is longer than the right from butt to bend

explanation: The correct answer is A (a twist in the front, leaving the two lens planes out of line): when one lens plane is rotated relative to the other, that side sits closer to the face, and the fault would have been caught by sighting along the front on the bench before fitting began. It is corrected at the bridge, not by bending a temple. Screw tension holds a lens in its groove and does not rotate the front. Unequal splay would show as uneven pad marks, which the stem rules out. A longer temple on one side changes where the bend falls at the ear, and both bends are stated to be equal.

question: Within the front itself the candidate has two faults to fix on the examiner: the front is crooked from side to side and the pantoscopic tilt is far too shallow. Which should be done first, and what is the reason for that order?

options.A: Tilt first, because tilt is set at the endpieces and level at the bridge
options.B: Tilt first, because tilt decides where the pupils fall inside the lenses
options.C: Level first, because tilt is judged against a front that is already square
options.D: Level first, because tilt cannot be changed once the frame is on a face

explanation: The correct answer is C (level first, because tilt is judged against a front that is already square): the accepted habit is horizontal before vertical, since a front that is still crooked gives two different apparent tilts on the two sides and there is no reliable reference to set the angle against. Once the front is square, equal tilt can be set at the two endpieces and confirmed from the side. Setting tilt first simply means resetting it after the front is straightened. Tilt does not decide horizontal level, and it can certainly be adjusted with the frame on the face, which is exactly where it is judged.

question: A patient's plastic frame needs the temple bend moved back by six millimetres so it starts at the top of the ear, in a station where the patient gives no feedback. The temples are a solid zyl with a wire core. What must the candidate do before making the bend?

options.A: Chill the temple so the zyl holds the new shape immediately
options.B: Warm the temple in the frame warmer until the zyl is supple
options.C: Loosen the hinge screw so the temple can rotate while bending
options.D: Remove the lens on that side to protect it from the pliers

explanation: The correct answer is B (warm the temple in the frame warmer until the zyl is supple): cellulose acetate has to be softened before it will take a new curve, and bending it cold splits the material or cracks it around the wire core. Warm in short passes and test pliability with the fingers rather than trusting a timer. Chilling the material makes it more brittle and more likely to break. Loosening the hinge screw lets the temple swing but does nothing about the stiffness of the material at the point being bent. Lenses are not removed to reshape a temple end, though the heat should be kept away from them.

question: After insertion, a candidate sights around the bevel line of a mounted lens and sees the apex standing proud of the groove for about ten millimetres along the lower temporal edge. The rest of the circumference looks fully seated. What does this finding mean?

options.A: The lens is undersized and is sliding within the eyewire groove
options.B: The bevel was cut too shallow and cannot reach the groove
options.C: The lens is not fully seated and must be reheated and reseated
options.D: The frame is overheated and the groove has closed at that point

explanation: The correct answer is C (the lens is not fully seated and must be reheated and reseated): a partly seated lens is held only by friction along the sections that did go in, so it can spring out under normal handling and it cannot be trusted to hold axis. The fix is to warm that eyewire again and roll the section over the bevel until the apex is buried in the groove around the whole circumference. An undersized lens rattles and spins rather than standing proud along one specific stretch of edge. A bevel cut too shallow or a groove closed by overheating would show a poor fit right around the lens, not one local failure.

question: A candidate holds a newly inserted plastic frame up to the light and looks through each lens for optical faults created by the insertion. Which finding indicates that the lens is under mechanical load from the frame and needs attention before dispensing?

options.A: Coloured stress patterns visible at the edge under crossed polarizers
options.B: A slight yellow cast across the whole surface of the lens
options.C: A ring of surface haze around the geometric centre of the lens
options.D: Fine concentric circles left across the surface by the edger wheel

explanation: The correct answer is A (coloured stress patterns visible at the edge under crossed polarizers): a lens squeezed by an eyewire that is too small becomes birefringent under load, and the strain shows as coloured fringes concentrated where the pressure is highest, usually at the corners. Strain like that means the lens is fighting the frame, so it will craze, chip, or crack in service and the lens must be reduced or recut before dispensing. A yellow cast is a material or tint characteristic and carries no information about load. Central haze and fine tooling circles are surfacing and finishing faults that were present before the lens ever met the frame.

question: An eyewire screw on a metal frame is missing and the candidate selects a replacement from the spares box. The new screw threads in, holds the eyewire closed, and protrudes about two millimetres below the barrel. What should be done before the frame is returned to the patient?

options.A: Leave the excess in place so the screw can be gripped later
options.B: Back the screw out one full turn to relieve the thread load
options.C: Grind the barrel flush with the screw head using a rotary tool
options.D: Trim the excess close to the barrel and peen or lock it

explanation: The correct answer is D (trim the excess close to the barrel and peen or lock it): a screw of correct diameter and thread but excess length is finished by cutting the protruding tail close to the barrel, after which the end is either peened slightly or treated with a retaining compound so it cannot back out. Trimming is not optional, because the compound does nothing about the shank standing proud. Either method keeps the eyewire closed and the lens secure between visits. A protruding tail scratches the patient's face and catches on cloths and cases, so leaving it is not acceptable. Backing the screw out loosens the eyewire and lets the lens rotate, and grinding the barrel destroys frame material to solve a screw length problem.

question: A metal frame arrives with a bridge that has snapped cleanly at the solder joint. The frame is a titanium alloy front, still under two years old, and the patient wants it repaired in house. What is the correct assessment of this repair?

options.A: Standard silver solder works on titanium if the joint is fluxed well
options.B: Any metal frame can be soldered once the lenses are removed first
options.C: Titanium will not take conventional solder and needs specialist laser welding
options.D: Heating the joint enough to solder it will always crack the plating

explanation: The correct answer is C (titanium will not take conventional solder and needs specialist laser welding): titanium forms an oxide layer instantly at soldering temperature, so ordinary silver solder and flux cannot bond to it and any joint made that way fails under normal wear. Frames of this material go to a laboratory with laser welding equipment, or the patient is advised honestly that replacement is the realistic option. Heavier fluxing does not change the metallurgy. It is not true that every metal frame can be soldered, and plating damage, while a real risk on plated base metal frames, is not the reason a titanium bridge cannot be soldered.

question: A patient collects a new pair of spectacles and the frame fits well at the dispensing. The patient asks whether anything else is needed now that the glasses have been handed over. What is the correct advice about ongoing care of the eyewear?

options.A: No further visits are needed unless the prescription itself changes later
options.B: Return only if a lens loosens or a screw actually falls out
options.C: Minor bending at home is acceptable provided the frame is warmed first
options.D: Book a follow up, since a frame drifts out of adjustment with wear

explanation: The correct answer is D (book a follow up, since a frame drifts out of adjustment with wear): daily handling, heat, and one handed removal move a frame away from the fit it left with, and a drifted fit changes optical centre height and vertex distance as well as comfort. Scheduling the return at dispensing makes it routine rather than something the patient has to decide to ask for. Continuing care is part of the optician's obligation and not an extra service, so telling the patient to stay away until the prescription changes abandons the fit. Waiting for a lens to fall out means the damage has already happened, and home bending is how fronts get twisted and temples get snapped.

question: At the dispensing visit an optician demonstrates how to take the spectacles off and how to clean them. The patient normally removes glasses with one hand and wipes them on a shirt tail. Which pair of instructions addresses the two faults most directly?

options.A: Remove with either hand, and dry polish with any soft tissue
options.B: Remove by the bridge, and clean with hot water and detergent
options.C: Remove by one temple only, and use a lens cloth when dry
options.D: Remove with two hands, and clean with lens solution and cloth

explanation: The correct answer is D (remove with two hands, and clean with lens solution and cloth): one handed removal pulls the front sideways every time and is the most common reason a frame that was symmetrical at dispensing comes back twisted within a month. Dry wiping on clothing drags trapped grit across the surface and is what puts fine scratches into a coated lens, so a proper solution and a clean lens cloth are used instead. Tissue is still a dry abrasive no matter which hand removed the frame. Pulling on the bridge loads a soldered or moulded joint, hot water can craze a coating, and removing by a single temple simply repeats the original fault.

question: During insertion a candidate hears a small click and finds a shallow chip on the edge of the right lens, sitting inside the eyewire groove where it cannot be seen once the lens is fully seated. The lens is otherwise correct in every respect.

options.A: Seat the lens fully, since a chip hidden in the groove cannot affect the wearer
options.B: Seat the lens and note the chip on the work order for future reference
options.C: Treat the lens as damaged, because a chip in the groove can spread under stress
options.D: File the chipped area smooth and then seat the lens into the eyewire

explanation: The correct answer is C (treat the lens as damaged, because a chip in the groove can spread under stress): an edge chip is a stress concentration, and the eyewire grips exactly there, so the crack can travel later while the patient is wearing the pair. Being invisible does not make it stable. Recording it without acting still sends out a compromised lens. Filing the edge alters the shape the eyewire was cut for and does not remove the underlying flaw.

question: A patient telephones two days after collecting a first pair of progressive lenses. The distance vision is clear and comfortable, but the patient reports having to turn the head to find the clear part of the page when reading, and finds this tiring.

options.A: Advise that progressive lenses are unsuitable and arrange a bifocal remake
options.B: Advise that nothing can be done until at least six weeks have passed
options.C: Refer the patient back to the prescriber for a repeat eye examination
options.D: Explain that this is normal early adaptation and arrange a follow up check

explanation: The correct answer is D (explain that this is normal early adaptation and arrange a follow up check): learning to point the nose at the target is exactly what a new progressive wearer must get used to, and clear distance vision suggests the fitting is sound. Bringing the patient in lets you verify the heights rather than guess. Abandoning the design after two days is premature. Refusing to look at it for six weeks abandons the patient. Nothing here suggests the prescription itself is wrong.

question: A candidate has finished a job and is arranging what happens next for the patient. The spectacles fit well today, the powers verify correctly, and the patient has been shown how to handle and clean them before leaving the dispensary.

options.A: Tell the patient to return only if something actually goes wrong
options.B: Book the next appointment for the patient's following eye examination
options.C: Invite the patient back for a check and readjustment after a short period
options.D: Advise that no further visits are needed once the fit has been confirmed

explanation: The correct answer is C (invite the patient back for a check and readjustment after a short period): frames settle and adjustments move with normal wear, so a planned early review catches a slipping fit before it becomes a complaint and confirms the patient is getting on with the lenses. Waiting for a problem leaves small faults to become large ones. The next eye examination is a separate matter and is far too distant. Telling a patient never to return abandons continuing care.
